newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rifkind rebuts Kohl, says EMU could divide Europe.
newsitem.headline: Rifkind rebuts Kohl, says EMU could divide Europe.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday Chancellor Helmut Kohl was wrong on European integration and warned that the planned single currency might divide Europe for decades.

But his comments received a cool reception from German politicians, journalists and bureaucrats who roared with laughter during a speech when he said Britain was the least nationalist of all members of the European Union.

Rifkind, on a visit to stir up critical debate about Europe in one of the EU's most pro-European states, said many members were unclear whether they wanted a United States of Europe or the community of nation states which Britain prefers.
He said he did not agree with Kohl that further integration of the European Union was an issue of war and peace and the bloc had to move forward or it would stumble.
"I don't myself believe his analysis is correct," he said. "The new Europe is not the Europe of the 19th century."
Rifkind also warned against going ahead with one of Kohl's pet projects, economic and monetary union (EMU), with only a few participants.
"What the European Union is contemplating is a change that will not unite but divide its member states, against the intentions of its founding members," Rifkind said.
He told a news conference that European leaders must not lose touch with "what ordinary people in Britain or France or Germany or Italy are thinking and talking and saying".
Most of Rifkind's invited audience at the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, a think tank linked to Kohl's Christian Democrats, certainly did not agree with him.
"Rifkind comes across as very British, whereas we Germans see ourselves as Europeans, who want more integration," said one government bureaucrat, who declined to be named.
The foundation's executive president, Gert Langguth, said it disagreed with Rifkind on many points "but we must be polite, because the British are masters of politeness."
A few guests at least welcomed Rifkind's frankness.

"There is no debate anymore in Germany. If you say anything you are labelled a bad European. Rifkind's approach is much more pragmatic than the high theory we have here," retired soldier Uwe Voegel said.

Rifkind said the German view of a more integrated union "looks like an agenda for creating a European state" and criticised Bonn's support for more EU majority voting as a potential threat to democracy itself.

Shortly after his arrival, Rifkind met CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble and his deputy Rudolf Seiters, two key pro-European strategists. He said they had had a good talk but could not say whether he had changed any minds.
Rifkind's speech was crafted with an eye to British politics, where European issues are likely to play a large part in campaigning ahead of a general election expected on May 1.

The Conservatives, some 18 points behind the opposition Labour Party according to the latest polls, believe they can win votes by portraying themselves as more determined to avoid the erosion of British sovereignty by the EU.

But Rifkind risked plunging his party into disarray over its stance on a single European currency, when he stood by comments made earlier on BBC radio that the British government was basically hostile to EMU.
"On balance we are hostile to a single currency, but we accept you have to think very carefully about these matters before you rule them out completely," he said.
But Rifkind stressed that he had used the word to describe Britain's position on a fudged start to the euro.
